330.title: Looking back
330.hook: stories, practices, portions, sayings, tales and songs: a year of Jewish life
330.tomorrow: year one close: the big lookout
330.howItsDone: The portion Masei, read each summer, lists all the Israelites' stops in the wilderness, and many Jews use the weeks before Rosh Hashanah to look back over the year that has passed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last line of the Book of Psalms. Your line was everything that breathes. Did a breath become a thank-you? Today, we stop and look back at the whole year. Day three hundred thirty.

When you climb a long hill, you mostly look down. At your feet, at the next step, at the rock you might trip on. It's only when you stop near the top and turn around that you see it: the whole path winding up behind you, the town tiny at the bottom, the place where you almost turned back. You didn't feel yourself climbing that far. But there it is. Today is that moment. We stop, turn around, and look at a year of Jewish life. Today: looking back.
screen: `EYES ON YOUR FEET.` → `STOP NEAR THE TOP AND TURN.` → `THE WHOLE PATH BEHIND YOU.`

segments.voice: The Torah itself does this. Near the end of the Book of Numbers, just before the Israelites reach the promised land, it stops and lists every place they camped in the wilderness. Forty-two stops, one after another. It could look like a boring list. But Rashi, the great commentator, passes on a parable. A king's son was sick, and his father took him far away to be healed. On the way home, the father pointed out each place: here we slept, here we were cold, here you had a headache. The list is love. It says: every stop counted. So let's name ours. We started with first words: shalom, the Shema, Shabbat, bracha, tzedakah, teshuvah. Then the stories: creation, Abraham, Jacob's long road, Joseph, the Exodus, the sea, Sinai. Then the practices: Shabbat candles, blessings through the day, the holidays as they came, tefillin, kashrut, study as prayer. Then the text, one portion at a time, from Bereshit into Exodus. And then the depths: the sayings of Pirkei Avot, be a mensch, don't judge until you've been there. A taste of Talmud: Hillel on one foot, Honi and his carob tree, these and these. The Hasidic tales: the shepherd boy's whistle, Zusya, the narrow bridge, the rebbe with the axe. And the Psalms, all the way to everything that breathes. You didn't feel yourself climbing this far. Some days you missed. Some days you only half listened. That's fine. The Torah lists the hard stops too. Look how far.
screen: `FORTY-TWO STOPS IN THE WILDERNESS.` · `HERE WE SLEPT, HERE WE WERE COLD.` · `WORDS, STORIES, PRACTICES, TEXT.` · `SAYINGS, TALES AND SONGS.` · then, large: `LOOK HOW FAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: list five things you've kept. Settle, and breathe. Let the year play back. Don't try to remember everything. Let five things come up that stayed with you. A word. A story. A practice you actually do now. A line you've said to someone else. A moment that changed how you see something. Count them on your fingers, one by one. If you have paper nearby, write them down afterward. If you pray, you can give thanks for each one. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. The Torah stops before the promised land to name every place the people camped. Here we slept. Here we were cold. Every stop counted.
Your line: look how far. Today, tell one person one thing you've learned this year, and notice how far you've come to be able to say it. Day three hundred thirty.

screen: `DAY 330 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YEAR ONE CLOSE: THE BIG LOOKOUT.`

331.title: Year one close: the big lookout
331.hook: the cycle turns on; next year, the rest of the Torah and the prayer book
331.carry: you kept me alive for this
331.tomorrow: Year two opens: back in the cycle
331.howItsDone: Many Jews say the Shehecheyanu blessing on the first night of a festival, over the first fruit of a season, for new clothes or a new home, and at personal milestones, thanking God for bringing them to this moment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back: stories, practices, portions, sayings, tales and songs. Your line was look how far. Did you find your five things? Today, the last step of year one. Day three hundred thirty-one.

There's a moment at the top of a long hike when you stop looking at your feet. For hours it was the next rock, the next root, the next switchback. Then the trail opens onto a ledge, and you turn around. The parking lot is a speck. The stream you crossed is a thread. The steep part that nearly made you quit is just a fold in the hill. You walked all that. Jewish tradition has a blessing for a moment exactly like this one, a few Hebrew words for simply having arrived. Today we stand at the big lookout, say what we see, and learn that blessing.
screen: `EYES ON YOUR FEET.` → `THE LEDGE.` → `A BLESSING FOR ARRIVING.`

segments.voice: Camp one was first words. Shalom, hello, goodbye and peace. The Shema, six words. Shabbat, sometimes called the oldest labor law. A bracha before eating. Tzedakah, which isn't charity but justice. Teshuvah, return. Camp two was the stories, the original serial: the world made and called good, Abraham arguing with God about Sodom, Jacob limping away renamed, Joseph, the sea, Sinai, and a portable tabernacle built from everyone's gifts. Camp three was the practices: holy time instead of holy place, blessings through the day, the holidays as they came, tefillin, kashrut, and study as a kind of prayer. Camp four read the weekly portion closely, from Bereshit to Va'era, fourteen portions, and stopped at hail with fire flashing inside it. And camp five went underneath: the sayings of the sages in Pirkei Avot, a taste of Talmud, Hasidic tales, and the Psalms, ending with everything that breathes. Now the blessing. It's called Shehecheyanu, from its key word, and the Mishnah already knows it: someone who builds a new house or buys new things says it. Today Jews say it on the first night of a festival, over the first fruit of a season, for new clothes, for a baby, for a milestone. In English it blesses God who has kept us alive, sustained us, and brought us to this season. That's all. No achievement required. You didn't have to climb well. You only had to arrive. And the year doesn't end with a finish line, because Jewish reading never really ends. When the last word of the Torah is read, the first word is read right after. Next year picks up where camp four stopped, reads the Torah through to its very last word, and opens the prayer book page by page. Psalm 118, one of the Hallel psalms, says it in the old Jewish translation: "This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it."
screen: `CAMP ONE: FIRST WORDS.` · `CAMPS TWO AND THREE: STORIES, PRACTICES.` · `CAMPS FOUR AND FIVE: PORTIONS, DEPTHS.` · `SHEHECHEYANU: KEPT ALIVE, BROUGHT HERE.` · then, large: `THIS IS THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: mark the arrival. Settle, and breathe. Let the year pass in front of you, like the view from the ledge. Don't grade it. Some days you were here with your whole heart, some days half asleep. You still arrived. If you pray, you can say Shehecheyanu now, in Hebrew or in English, for having reached this day. If you don't pray, just name, quietly, one thing that carried you here: a person, a habit, plain stubbornness. Then let the thanks sit in your chest for a while. The bell holds the time.
Year one close. Not a finish line but a lookout: you turn around, see the whole climb, bless the arriving, and face the path again.

Your line: you kept me alive for this. Today, notice one new or first thing, a taste, a season, a moment, and let that line go through your head. Tomorrow the scroll keeps rolling. Day three hundred thirty-one.

screen: `DAY 331 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YEAR TWO OPENS: BACK IN THE CYCLE.`

332.title: Year two opens: back in the cycle
332.hook: last year stopped at Va'era; this year the Torah is read through to its last word
332.howItsDone: Synagogues read one Torah portion each Shabbat, in order, across the year; on Simchat Torah the last lines of Deuteronomy are read and the first lines of Genesis follow at once. Many Jews study the week's portion at home as well.

segments.voice: Yesterday we stood at the big lookout and blessed the arriving. Your line was you kept me alive for this. Did one first thing of the day get that line? Now the path turns into year two. Day three hundred thirty-two.

A Torah scroll is two wooden rollers with a long ribbon of parchment wound between them, and fully unrolled it would run longer than a city bus. On Shabbat morning someone opens it on the reading table, and it's already sitting where last week's reading stopped. Nobody rewinds to the start because they missed a week. Nobody skips ahead to the good part. The scroll simply waits at the place it was left. Last year our reading stopped in the middle of Exodus, in a portion called Va'era, with hail and fire falling on Egypt together. Year two picks up from exactly there.
screen: `TWO ROLLERS, ONE LONG RIBBON.` → `IT WAITS WHERE YOU LEFT IT.` → `WE STOPPED AT VA'ERA.`

segments.voice: The Torah, the five books of Moses, is divided into fifty-four weekly portions. Each one is called a parashah, which simply means a section; plenty of people say parsha. Each portion is named for an early, distinctive word in it. Bereshit, in the beginning. Va'era, and I appeared. Next comes Bo, which means come. Across the Jewish year the portions are read one after another, and in weeks when the calendar runs short, two are read together so the whole thing fits. The annual cycle grew up among the Jews of Babylonia. The Talmud remembers that Jews in the Land of Israel took about three years to finish, and today some congregations read a third of each portion, a three-year rhythm with ancient roots. Either way, the end is not an end. On the holiday of Simchat Torah, the last lines of Deuteronomy are read, and straight after them, the first lines of Genesis. People dance with the scrolls in their arms. The circle closes and opens in the same morning. The sayings of the fathers keep a line from a sage called Ben Bag Bag about the Torah: turn it and turn it, for everything is in it. A year-two reader turns it again. Here's the plan. First, the rest of Exodus, Bo to the finished tabernacle. Then Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, to the very last word. Then the siddur, the prayer book, page by page. Then the Jewish year, in depth.
screen: `FIFTY-FOUR PORTIONS: PARASHAH.` · `NAMED FOR AN EARLY WORD.` · `ONE YEAR, OR THREE.` · `SIMCHAT TORAH: THE END MEETS THE START.` · then, large: `TURN IT AND TURN IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your place in the cycle. Settle, and breathe. Picture the scroll lying open at the spot where you left it, waiting, not annoyed that you were gone. Think of one thing in your own life you set down and meant to pick up again: a book, a habit, a conversation. Don't scold yourself. Just notice where your marker is. After the bell, if you like, look up which portion synagogues read this coming Shabbat. Any Jewish calendar lists it. The bell holds the time.
Year two opens. We pick up the Torah where we left it, at Bo, and read through to the last word, then open the prayer book.
Your line: the scroll keeps rolling. Today, pick up one thing you set down, right where you left it, without starting over. Day three hundred thirty-two.

333.title: Bo: come, not go (Exodus 10:1)
333.hook: God tells Moses "come unto Pharaoh", as if God is already in the room
333.tomorrow: Bo: darkness that could be felt (Exodus 10:21–23)
333.howItsDone: Bo is read in synagogues in midwinter, usually in January. Many teachers and Hasidic commentators dwell on its first word, reading 'come' as a sign that God goes ahead of Moses into Pharaoh's palace.

segments.voice: Yesterday year two opened. Your line was the scroll keeps rolling. Did you pick something up where you left it? Today the scroll rolls into a new portion, and its very first word. Day three hundred thirty-three.

There's a difference between a coach who says go out there and one who says come on, out we go. Same field. Same game. But one of them is staying on the bench, and the other one is walking out beside you. Moses has stood before Pharaoh again and again. Seven plagues have come. Each time, Pharaoh ends up saying no. Moses has every reason to dread going back. And the portion opens with God sending him back, using a word that, in Hebrew, is a little strange. It isn't the word for go. It's the word for come.
screen: `GO OUT THERE, OR COME ON.` → `SEVEN PLAGUES, STILL NO.` → `NOT GO. COME.`

segments.voice: The portion is named for that word: Bo. In Hebrew, God says to Moses, bo el Par'oh. Most English translations, the old Jewish one included, smooth it into go in unto Pharaoh, and that's fair: the Hebrew verb can mean entering. But its plain sense is come. And people who speak to you as come are usually already where they're asking you to be. The Zohar, the great book of Jewish mysticism, plays with exactly this. It pictures God leading Moses inward, room after room, into the innermost chamber of Pharaoh's power, the place Moses was most afraid of, and saying: come. Not go there alone. Come here, where I already am. It's a reading, not the plain story, and the Zohar wraps it in a lot of symbolism about the deep places of evil. But the simple point has traveled far beyond the mystics. Back at the burning bush, Moses had asked who he was to stand before Pharaoh. God's answer then was the shortest promise in the book: "Certainly I will be with thee." Bo is that promise, folded into one syllable. It doesn't make the room less hard. Pharaoh will still say no. The verse even says, right there, that his heart has been hardened. Moses still has to walk in. He just doesn't walk in first.
screen: `BO EL PAR'OH: COME UNTO PHARAOH.` · `COME: SOMEONE IS ALREADY THERE.` · `THE ZOHAR: ROOM AFTER ROOM.` · `I WILL BE WITH THEE.` · then, large: `COME, NOT GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse a hard room. Settle, and breathe. Think of a room you're dreading this week. A meeting, a phone call, a doctor's office, a kitchen where an old argument lives. Picture the door. Now picture walking through it, not as the first one in, but as someone being called in, by a voice already inside. If you pray, you can hold the words I will be with thee as you cross the threshold. If not, just picture one person who'd be on your side in there. Stay with that doorway. The bell holds the time.
Bo. Come. The name of this week's portion, and the word God uses to send Moses back to Pharaoh, as if calling him into a room God is already in.
Your line: come, not go. Today, when you walk into the hardest room on your list, say it under your breath at the door. Day three hundred thirty-three.

334.title: Bo: darkness that could be felt (Exodus 10:21–23)
334.hook: three days so dark "they saw not one another"; yet in Israel's homes there was light
334.howItsDone: The ten plagues are recited at the Passover seder, a drop of wine spilled for each, and darkness is the ninth. Jewish tradition counts visiting and checking on people who are ill or grieving, bikur cholim and comforting mourners, as a mitzvah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the portion's first word, bo. Your line was come, not go. Which hard room did you walk into, and did you say it at the door? Today, the ninth plague. Day three hundred thirty-four.

During a power cut at night, the first thing most people do isn't look for a flashlight. It's call out. Are you okay? Where are you? Darkness doesn't only hide the furniture. It hides the people. The ninth plague is darkness, and the Torah describes it in a way that sounds less like night and more like a weight. It came after the locusts, it lasted three days, and the most striking line about it isn't about the sky at all. It's about what people could no longer see in each other.
screen: `THE POWER CUT.` → `ARE YOU OKAY?` → `THE NINTH PLAGUE.`

segments.voice: Moses stretches out his hand toward heaven, and a thick darkness covers Egypt. The old Jewish translation calls it "darkness which may be felt." Darkness you could touch. Then comes the detail. For three days, "they saw not one another, neither rose any from his place." Not just: they couldn't see the road. They couldn't see each other. And because they couldn't see each other, nobody got up. There's a teaching often told in Hasidic circles that reads those two halves as cause and effect. The darkest darkness, it says, is when a person doesn't see his brother. When you stop seeing the person next to you, you stop being able to move. You stay stuck in your place. The verse ends with a turn: "but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings." The Torah doesn't explain how. Commentators offered many answers, and the plain text stays quiet. But notice where the light was: in their dwellings, in homes, among people. The midrash also wonders why the darkness had to last three days, and gives several reasons; none of them is in the verse itself. What the verse does give is the picture: one land where nobody could see anybody, and homes where people could. A dark time can be a whole country's or one person's. Grief does it. Depression does it. A long illness, a lost job. The person inside often can't rise from their place. Someone else, with light, can see them.
screen: `DARKNESS WHICH MAY BE FELT.` · `THEY SAW NOT ONE ANOTHER.` · `NOT SEEING, SO NOT RISING.` · `LIGHT IN THEIR DWELLINGS.` · then, large: `SEE YOUR BROTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for someone in the dark. Settle, and breathe. Let a few faces come to mind, the people in your life right now. Who's had the lights go out lately? A friend who's gone quiet. A neighbor after a loss. A relative who's stopped answering. Let one face stay. You don't have to fix anything. Just see them, properly, the way you'd call out in a power cut. If you pray, you can hold them there for a while. After the bell, send one short message: thinking of you. The bell holds the time.
Bo. Still our portion. Today its ninth plague: darkness so thick no one could see another person, and light in Israel's homes.
Your line: see your brother. Brother, sister, friend, stranger. Today, check on one person who's in a dark stretch, and let them know they've been seen. Day three hundred thirty-four.

335.title: Bo: this month is yours (Exodus 12:1–2)
335.hook: the first command to the whole people is to mark time by the new moon
335.howItsDone: Jews mark Rosh Chodesh, the new month, with added prayers including Hallel, and in synagogue the coming new month is announced on the Shabbat before. Some people also say a blessing over the waxing moon each month, Kiddush Levanah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the darkness you could feel, and homes that still had light. Your line was see your brother. Did you check on someone? Today, still in Bo, the moon. Day three hundred thirty-five.

Look at a work schedule someone else wrote for you. Shifts, breaks, the hour you may leave. Now imagine that for your whole life, and your parents' lives, every hour belonged to someone else. That's slavery's calendar: the master owns the clock. The plagues are almost over. One more, the worst, is coming. And right here, before anyone has left Egypt, God gives Moses and Aaron the first command meant for the whole people. You might expect something about freedom, or worship, or the law. It's about the moon.
screen: `A SCHEDULE SOMEONE ELSE WROTE.` → `THE MASTER OWNS THE CLOCK.` → `THE FIRST COMMAND: THE MOON.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the old Jewish translation: "This month shall be unto you the beginning of months; it shall be the first month of the year to you." The Hebrew word for month is chodesh, from the same root as chadash, new. A month is a new moon, a renewal. From that verse comes the whole Jewish calendar, a lunar calendar adjusted to the sun so the spring festival stays in spring. In ancient times the new month was declared by a court in Jerusalem, after witnesses came to say they had seen the thin new crescent. Later the calendar was fixed by calculation, which is how it runs today. And the first day of each month, Rosh Chodesh, is still marked with extra prayers. Rashi, the great medieval commentator, opens his whole commentary on the Torah with a question about this verse. Why, he asks, didn't the Torah simply begin here, with this month, the first command given to Israel? He has his own answer, about the land. But his question tells you how weighty this verse was to him. Sforno, an Italian commentator of the sixteenth century, noticed the small word unto you. Until now, he says, their days belonged to others. From here on, the months are theirs. Before a free people can do anything else, it has to own its time.
screen: `THIS MONTH SHALL BE UNTO YOU.` · `CHODESH: MONTH, FROM NEW.` · `WITNESSES, THEN A FIXED CALENDAR.` · `SFORNO: THE MONTHS ARE YOURS.` · then, large: `OWN YOUR TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: claim today. Settle, and breathe. Say today's date to yourself, the day of the week, the month, the year. Not as a deadline. As a fact you're choosing to notice. Then ask: which hours today are mine to shape? Maybe not many. Maybe ten minutes on a bus. Pick one stretch and decide, now, what it's for. If you know the Hebrew date, say that too. If you pray, you can offer that stretch of time. The bell holds the time.
Bo. Our portion still. Today, its first command to a people not yet free: count your months by the new moon. Time becomes theirs.
Your line: own your time. Today, mark the date on purpose: write it at the top of a page, or look up at the moon tonight and see where it is. Day three hundred thirty-five.

336.title: Bo: tell your child (Exodus 13:8)
336.hook: "thou shalt tell thy son in that day", the root of the seder's telling
336.tomorrow: Bo: a sign upon your hand (Exodus 13:9, 16)
336.howItsDone: At the Passover seder, Jewish families read the Haggadah together: children ask four questions, the Exodus is retold with food, songs and four cups of wine, and the passage of the four children is read aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday a people still in Egypt was handed its own calendar. Your line was own your time. Did you mark the date on purpose? Today, the last night in Egypt turns into a story. Day three hundred thirty-six.

Every family has one story that gets told at every holiday. The time the car broke down in the snow. How Grandma crossed the border with one suitcase. The kids roll their eyes, and then, one year, a kid tells it themselves, and gets the details slightly wrong, and someone corrects them, and that's how you know it's alive. The Torah sees this coming. Before the Israelites have even left Egypt, before the sea, before Sinai, it's already planning how the story will be told to children who weren't there.
screen: `THE STORY TOLD EVERY HOLIDAY.` → `ONE YEAR, A KID TELLS IT.` → `PLANNED BEFORE THE EXODUS.`

segments.voice: The verse, in the old Jewish translation, begins: "And thou shalt tell thy son in that day." The Hebrew for and thou shalt tell is v'higadta, from the verb l'haggid, to tell. And from that verb comes today's word: haggadah, the telling. It's the name of the little book on every table at the Passover seder, the script for retelling the Exodus, with questions, songs, food you eat for the story's sake. The Torah talks about children asking about the Exodus in four places, and the rabbis noticed each one sounds different. So the Haggadah sets four children around the table: one wise, one wicked, one simple, and one who doesn't know how to ask. Our verse belongs to that fourth child. Nobody asked a question here. The parent just begins. The Haggadah says, in effect: for the one who can't ask, you open the story for them. Then look at the rest of the verse. The parent says the LORD did this for me, when I came out of Egypt. For me. Not for our ancestors. The Mishnah turns that into a rule: in every generation, a person should see themselves as if they personally came out of Egypt. That's why the Haggadah is a telling, not a history lesson. Each generation tells it as its own story, so the next one can.
screen: `V'HIGADTA: AND THOU SHALT TELL.` · `HAGGADAH: THE TELLING.` · `FOUR CHILDREN, ONE WHO CAN'T ASK.` · `FOR ME, AS IF I CAME OUT.` · then, large: `TELL YOUR CHILD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the story you'd tell. Settle, and breathe. Think of one story from your family, or from your own life, that a younger person should know. How someone arrived. How something was survived. A kindness that changed things. Let it play through once in your head, the way you'd actually say it out loud. Notice where you'd say we, and where you'd say I. If no children are in your life, think of a niece, a student, a younger friend. The bell holds the time.
Haggadah. The telling. From the verb in thou shalt tell thy son, and the name of the book read at the Passover seder.

Your line: tell your child. A week into year two: come, not go, the darkness, the moon, and now the telling. Today, tell a younger person one family story, even a short one. Day three hundred thirty-six.
